{"dialogue": "Rufus, here is something that stopped me when I read the engineering write-up. When Anthropic rewrote the backbone of their own Messages API, the thing that actually processes requests to Claude, they did not take it offline to test whether the new version behaved identically to the old one. They ran both versions simultaneously, in sandboxes, with agents comparing the outputs.
RUFUS: So they used Claude to check the work of the system that runs Claude.
JAMIE: That is precisely what happened. And I want to be careful about how I frame that, because it sounds like it could go sideways very fast.
ALEX: It sounds like asking someone to proofread their own diary.
JAMIE: Except the diary is a live API with real production traffic behind it, so the stakes for a typo are somewhat higher than embarrassment.
RUFUS: Jamie's AI Transformation. The segment where Jamie opens with a software engineering detail and I realize I need to pay closer attention than I expected.
JAMIE: You say that like I gave you a choice.
ALEX: He really did not have one.
RUFUS: Neither did I, apparently. Alright, back up. What is the Messages API and why does rewriting it matter?
JAMIE: The Messages API is the interface that developers use to send requests to Claude and receive responses. It is the layer that handles the actual traffic. Anthropic decided to rewrite it in Rust, which is a programming language known for memory safety and performance. The original was not in Rust. Moving to Rust meant rewriting the code that handles every incoming request, and doing that without introducing behavioral differences that break things for the developers relying on it.
ALEX: And the problem is verifying that the new version behaves exactly like the old one.
JAMIE: That is the crux. You can read both versions of the code and convince yourself they should be equivalent. But at the edges, the cases that only come up under specific input conditions, that conviction can be wrong. The question is how you catch the differences you did not anticipate.
RUFUS: Which is where the agents come in.
JAMIE: Claude agents compared the two versions in sandboxes. They generated inputs, ran them against both the old and new implementations, and flagged wherever the outputs diverged. When they found a difference, engineers reviewed it before anything moved forward. The agents did the systematic comparison work. The engineers made the judgment calls about what the differences meant and what needed fixing. After that review stage, the validated version went through shadow-traffic testing against real production patterns.
ALEX: Shadow traffic meaning real requests hitting both systems in parallel, with the new system not actually serving the responses yet.
JAMIE: Right. It is a staged approach. Sandbox comparison with agents, human review of flagged differences, then shadow validation before the new system takes over live traffic.
RUFUS: And the result?
JAMIE: Anthropic reports completing the migration without service downtime. Public traffic moved in September 2026. The engineering write-up came out November 25th, 2026, which is where this account comes from. I want to be direct about the evidence: this is Anthropic's own engineering documentation. Anthropic is the company that built both the tool and the system being migrated. It is a single attributed source, not an independent measurement.
ALEX: So we believe it happened. We are just being honest that the entity telling us about it also made Claude.
JAMIE: That is the right frame. It is a vendor engineering account of an internal production migration. The technical approach is detailed and coherent. The source caveat stands.
RUFUS: I want to push on something, because passing a sandbox checker sounds like it should be sufficient. If the agents compared every output and found no differences, is that not just done?
JAMIE: This is the part of Anthropic's own write-up that I think is worth dwelling on, and they are quite direct about it. Passing the local checker did not by itself establish that shipping was the right decision. Human review remained a necessary layer. The engineers were not simply ratifying whatever the agents found. They were applying judgment about whether the differences mattered, whether the test cases were representative, whether something might have been missed.
ALEX: The agents cannot know what they did not think to test.
JAMIE: Exactly. The agent-driven comparison is systematic across the cases it covers. Human review is what catches the blind spots in the coverage itself. Those are different functions and both of them were part of this workflow.
RUFUS: So the agent closes the volume gap and the engineer closes the judgment gap.
JAMIE: That is the division. And I think it is worth naming what this migration is not. It is one internal production rewrite at Anthropic. The write-up describes an engineering technique, not a universally available product. The internal migration infrastructure they built for this is not something you can go and deploy today.
ALEX: But the technique is published.
JAMIE: The technique is published. That is the thing that generalizes. The specific setup Anthropic used belongs to Anthropic. The principle, using agents to systematically compare behavioral outputs between versions while preserving human review before anything ships, that is a described approach anyone working on a comparable verification problem can think about.
RUFUS: Can I try a hypothetical? Say someone listening is not running API migrations but they have a team that updates internal data processing scripts fairly regularly. Same idea applies?
JAMIE: That is a reasonable place to draw the line to. Hypothetically, if you had old and new versions of a script that processes CSV exports and you wanted to catch behavioral differences before switching, you could construct something similar in structure. Create a set of synthetic edge cases covering the input conditions you care most about. Run both versions on those cases. Inspect the differences before accepting the new version as production-ready. That is not the same scale as what Anthropic did, and I want to be clear it is a proposed exercise, not a tested workflow I can point to results from. But the structure of the thinking maps.
ALEX: I like that as a concrete first step. It does not require any new tool. It just requires being deliberate about what you check before you switch.
RUFUS: Jamie, I have to ask, does it feel strange to cover a case where the AI company used their own AI to audit their own AI, and then published a write-up about it themselves?
JAMIE: It would feel stranger if the write-up were vague. The fact that Anthropic published specific technical details about where the approach worked and where human oversight remained necessary is actually what makes it worth reporting. A press release saying we migrated successfully with AI is not interesting. An engineering account that says the checker was not sufficient to make the shipping decision alone, that is a more honest document.
ALEX: They published their own limitation.
JAMIE: They published their own limitation. That is worth noting.
RUFUS: So the first move for someone listening who is thinking about version comparison in their own work is not to call Anthropic.
JAMIE: The first move is to be specific about what behavioral equivalence actually means for the thing you are changing. Write that down before you pick any tool. What outputs matter? Under what input conditions? Which edge cases have historically caused problems? If you cannot answer those questions concretely, automated comparison is not going to give you useful information, because you will not know whether the differences it finds are significant.
ALEX: Define the test before you run it.
JAMIE: Define the test before you run it. The reason I think this case changes how the business of building software works, not just one migration, is what it says about the verification bottleneck. The hard part of a live behavioral rewrite has always been the gap between reading the code and knowing it behaves identically in practice. Agent-driven comparison does not close that gap completely, as Anthropic is explicit about. But it narrows it systematically in a way that manual spot-checking does not.
RUFUS: And you still need a person on the other side of every flag.
JAMIE: You still need a person on the other side of every flag. The migration completed in September 2026. The engineering account is from Anthropic's own write-up published November 25th, 2026, at their research site. Single attributed source, internal production context, technique published, infrastructure not generally available. The agents did the comparing. The engineers did the deciding. The traffic moved without the lights going out.
ALEX: That last sentence is doing a lot of work.
JAMIE: It is meant to."}
